name: Alexander the Great
info: Alexander III of Macedon, known as Alexander the Great, was king of the ancient Greek kingdom of Macedon from 336 to 323 BCE, who conquered the Achaemenid Persian Empire and led his army as far as northwestern India.

facts.born: Probably 20 July 356 BCE (the exact date is uncertain) at Pella, capital of Macedon; son of King Philip II of the Argead dynasty and his fourth wife, Olympias of Epirus
facts.died: 10 or 11 June 323 BCE in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar II at Babylon, aged 32, after an illness of about twelve days; the ancient accounts differ on its course, and some alleged poison
facts.role: King of Macedon, 336–323 BCE; Hegemon of the League of Corinth and commander of the war against Persia from 336 BCE; crowned in the temple of Ptah at Memphis in Egypt; ruler of the conquered Achaemenid Empire
facts.known: the conquest of the Achaemenid Persian Empire; the battles of Issus, Gaugamela and the Hydaspes; never losing a battle; founding Alexandria in Egypt and more than twenty other cities; the spread of Greek language and culture and the beginning of the Hellenistic period; the legends gathered in the Alexander Romance

t: Heir to the army and the Greek alliance built by his father Philip II, Alexander became king of Macedon at 20 and in ten years of campaigning from 334 BCE overthrew the Achaemenid Persian Empire.

The conquests were made with massacres and enslavement at Thebes, Tyre, Gaza and Massaga, and his adoption of Persian customs and the killing of his own officers cost him the sympathy of many Macedonians.

He died at Babylon at 32 without an obvious heir; his generals fought for forty years over an empire that broke into Hellenistic kingdoms, through which Greek language and culture spread from Egypt to India.
dyk: Alexander's body was laid in a gold sarcophagus filled with honey. His companion Ptolemy seized the funeral cortege on its way to Macedon and took the body to Egypt, where a later king, Ptolemy IX Lathyros, replaced the gold sarcophagus with a glass one so that he could turn the original into coin.
ev: Alexander is born at Pella, the capital of Macedon, to King Philip II and Olympias
Philip II is assassinated at Aigai and Alexander is proclaimed king by the nobles and army at the age of 20
After a campaign in the Balkans he razes rebellious Thebes and divides its territory among the other Boeotian cities
His army crosses the Hellespont into Asia and defeats Persian forces at the Battle of the Granicus
He defeats Darius III at Issus; Darius flees, leaving behind his wife, daughters and mother
Victory over Darius at Gaugamela, the final and decisive encounter between the two, is followed by the capture of Babylon
He defeats King Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes in the Punjab, and his army mutinies at the Hyphasis, refusing to march farther east
Alexander dies at Babylon, aged 32, while planning an invasion of Arabia

sections.early:
Alexander III was born at Pella, the capital of the kingdom of Macedon, on a day that probably corresponds to 20 July 356 BCE, though the exact date is uncertain. His father was King Philip II of the Argead dynasty; his mother, Olympias, daughter of King Neoptolemus I of Epirus, was Philip's fourth wife and for some time his principal one. Through Philip he could claim descent from Heracles and through his mother's family from Achilles. The legends of his birth, among them the dreams that the biographer Plutarch reports and the story that Zeus was his father, may have emerged when Alexander was king, possibly at his own instigation.

He was raised in the manner of noble Macedonian youths, learning to read, play the lyre, ride, fight and hunt, under a nurse, Lanike, and the tutors Leonidas and Lysimachus of Acarnania. Plutarch tells how at ten he tamed a horse that had refused to be mounted; he named it Bucephalas, and it carried him as far as India. When Alexander was 13, Philip chose the philosopher Aristotle as his tutor and gave the Temple of the Nymphs at Mieza as a classroom. There Alexander studied with the sons of Macedonian nobles such as Ptolemy, Hephaestion and Cassander, many of them his future generals. Aristotle taught them medicine, philosophy, morals, religion, logic and art, and gave Alexander an annotated copy of the Iliad, which he later carried on his campaigns. Persian exiles living at Philip's court, among them Artabazos II, also gave the Macedonians a good knowledge of Persian affairs.
sections.rise:
Alexander's education under Aristotle ended at 16, when Philip, at war with the Thracians, left him as regent and heir apparent. He put down a revolt of the Thracian Maedi and founded a city, Alexandropolis, in their territory. In 338 BCE father and son met the armies of Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in Boeotia, where Philip commanded the right wing and Alexander the left; Alexander was the first to break the Theban lines. At Corinth Philip then formed the alliance of Greek states that modern scholars call the League of Corinth, was named its Hegemon and announced plans to attack the Persian Empire.

Philip's marriage in 338 BCE to Cleopatra Eurydice, niece of his general Attalus, made Alexander's position as heir less secure, since a son of hers would be fully Macedonian. After a quarrel at the wedding banquet Alexander fled in 337 BCE with his mother, returning after six months. In October 336 BCE Philip was assassinated at Aigai by Pausanias, the captain of his bodyguards, and the nobles and army proclaimed Alexander king on the spot, at the age of 20.

He began by eliminating potential rivals: his cousin Amyntas IV was executed, two princes of Lyncestis were killed, and he ordered the murder of Attalus. News of Philip's death roused Thebes, Athens, Thessaly and the Thracian tribes to revolt. Alexander rode south with 3,000 cavalry, outflanked the Thessalians, and at Corinth took the title of Hegemon and the command against Persia. In 335 BCE he secured his northern frontier in Thrace and Illyria, and when Thebes rebelled again he razed the city.
sections.deeds:
In 334 BCE Alexander's army crossed the Hellespont with approximately 48,100 soldiers, 6,100 cavalry and 120 ships. After a first victory at the Battle of the Granicus he accepted the surrender of Sardis, moved along the Ionian coast and took Halicarnassus by siege, seizing the coastal cities to deny the Persians naval bases. In 333 BCE he defeated Darius III at Issus; Darius fled, leaving his family behind, and offered peace and a ransom of 10,000 talents, which Alexander refused, replying that he was now king of Asia. Tyre fell in 332 BCE after a long siege, and Gaza after three failed assaults.

In Egypt, where he was regarded as a liberator, Alexander sacrificed to the gods at Memphis, was pronounced son of the god Amun by the oracle at the Siwa Oasis, and founded Alexandria. In 331 BCE he marched into Mesopotamia and defeated Darius again at Gaugamela, their final and decisive encounter, then took Babylon, the treasury of Susa and the ceremonial capital, Persepolis. Darius was stabbed on the orders of his satrap Bessus, and Alexander buried him in a regal funeral, claiming to have been named his successor.

The pursuit of Bessus, who was executed in 329 BCE, became a campaign across Central Asia, where Alexander founded a series of cities called Alexandria and married Roxana, daughter of a Sogdian nobleman. He then invaded the Indian subcontinent and in 326 BCE won the Battle of the Hydaspes against King Porus, whom he made an ally and satrap. He was never defeated in battle, despite typically being outnumbered.
sections.opponents:
The conquests were violent. At Tyre and at Gaza the men of military age were killed and the women and children sold into slavery, and the Roman historian Curtius writes that at Massaga Alexander slaughtered the entire population and reduced its buildings to rubble; a similar massacre followed at Ora. His troops looted Persepolis for several days, and a fire that began in the palace of Xerxes I spread through the city, by drunken accident or as deliberate revenge. Pre-Islamic Persian literature calls Alexander gujastak, "accursed", and accuses him of destroying temples and burning the sacred texts of Zoroastrianism.

Among his own men the gravest quarrels arose from his adoption of Persian dress and customs, notably proskynesis, a gesture the Greeks reserved for gods; he eventually abandoned it. After a plot was revealed, his officer Philotas was executed for failing to alert him, and Alexander ordered the assassination of Philotas's father, the general Parmenion. At Maracanda he personally killed Cleitus the Black, who had saved his life at the Granicus, in a drunken altercation in which Cleitus accused him of forgetting Macedonian ways. His official historian Callisthenes, who had led the opposition to proskynesis, was implicated in a plot of the royal pages; it remains unclear whether he was involved.

Some Roman writers used Alexander as a cautionary tale of autocratic tendencies and anger. In his final years he showed signs of megalomania and paranoia, though his behaviour may also have been a practical attempt to hold a culturally disparate empire together.
sections.last:
At the Hyphasis River in 326 BCE the army, exhausted by years of campaigning and fearing the large armies farther east, mutinied and refused to go on. Alexander turned south along the Indus; while besieging the citadel of the Mallians he was nearly killed by an arrow that entered his lung. He lost many men in the Gedrosian Desert and reached Susa in 324 BCE. He executed several satraps who had misbehaved in his absence, held a mass marriage of his senior officers to Persian and other noblewomen, and faced a second mutiny at Opis, where his troops criticised the introduction of Persian officers and soldiers into Macedonian units. At Ecbatana his closest friend, Hephaestion, died of illness or poisoning, which devastated him.

Back in Babylon, Alexander was planning an invasion of Arabia when he died in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar II on 10 or 11 June 323 BCE, at age 32. Plutarch describes a fever that worsened after a night and day of drinking; Diodorus writes of pain after a large bowl of unmixed wine and no fever. Several ancient writers mention a theory of poisoning, which Plutarch dismissed as a fabrication; malaria and typhoid fever are among the natural causes suggested.

He left no obvious heir: his son Alexander IV was born to Roxana after his death. According to Diodorus he bequeathed his kingdom "to the strongest"; other writers say he passed his signet ring to Perdiccas. Alexander IV and Alexander's half-brother Philip III were made joint kings in name only, and both were later murdered. Forty years of war among the Successors followed.
sections.legacy:
At his death Alexander's empire covered some 5,200,000 square kilometres and was the largest state of its time. Out of the wars of his generals came three stable powers, Ptolemaic Egypt, Seleucid Syria and Persia, and Antigonid Macedonia, and his death marks the conventional beginning of the Hellenistic period. He founded more than twenty cities, the first and greatest being Alexandria in Egypt. A common Greek dialect, koine, became the lingua franca of these lands, and the New Testament was written in it. In Afghanistan and India Greek culture mixed with Iranian and Buddhist cultures in what is known as Greco-Buddhism, while the power vacuum he left in the north-west of the Indian subcontinent gave rise to the Maurya Empire. His constant demands for troops, however, depleted Macedon itself, which was later subjugated by Rome.

Romans from Pompey to the emperor Caracalla took him as a model. The Alexander Romance, a text of legendary material, went through over one hundred recensions and translations across the European and Islamic worlds. Firdausi's Shahnameh places him in a line of legitimate Persian shahs, and most modern researchers believe the Qur'an's Dhu al-Qarnayn refers to him.

The accounts of those who knew Alexander are lost. The surviving histories, by Diodorus Siculus, Quintus Curtius Rufus, Arrian, Plutarch and Justin, were written centuries later; Arrian, who used Ptolemy and Aristobulus, is generally considered the most reliable. Many scholars doubt the historicity of the "last plans" for further conquest that Diodorus ascribes to him.

summary: Alexander the Great became king of Macedon in 336 BCE and in ten years of campaigning overthrew the Achaemenid Persian Empire, reaching Egypt, Central Asia and the Punjab without losing a battle. He died at Babylon in 323 BCE aged 32. His empire broke apart among his generals, but Greek language and culture spread across the lands he had conquered.
